rows.label: Household consumption per person, United States, 2024 (current US$)

source.title: World Bank, World Development Indicators: households and NPISHs final consumption expenditure (NE.CON.PRVT.CD) ÷ population (SP.POP.TOTL), 2024

rows.explainer: What an average person in the United States consumes in a year, the base a rich-country model's ln(consumption) gain is measured against (scaled to its recipients by the model's own share of the mean): the site's one log-income scale, so a dollar of food or housing does far less here than for a household living on a few dollars a day.

rows.label: Spending of the lowest-income fifth of US households, as a share of the average household's, 2024

source.title: BLS, Consumer Expenditures in 2024 (news release, 19 December 2025), Table C: average annual expenditures by income quintile
source.quote: average annual expenditures ranged from $35,046 for consumer units in the lowest income quintile
source.note: All consumer units $78,535; lowest quintile $35,046; 35,046 / 78,535 = 0.4462. Per consumer unit: the lowest quintile's units are smaller, so per person the ratio is higher.

rows.explainer: How much less the poorest fifth of US households spend than the average one, per household: the anchor for how far below the mean a US social service's clients consume (a model's recipients_consumption_share, judged per person from it).

rows.label: Population, United States, 2024

source.title: World Bank, World Development Indicators: population, total (SP.POP.TOTL), 2024

rows.explainer: The US population the site's per-person US figures divide by (the same figure as in consumption_per_person_2024): national rates per person, such as deaths in home fires or cardiac arrests a year.

rows.label: Value of an hour of volunteer time, United States, 2024 (US$)

source.title: University of Maryland Do Good Institute and Independent Sector, value of volunteer time for 2024 (brief, April 2025)
source.quote: The value of a volunteer hour is $34.79

rows.explainer: Independent Sector's value of a volunteer hour: the average hourly earnings of US private non-farm production and non-supervisory workers (BLS) plus fringe benefits. The local wage the site values unpaid US volunteer and trainee time at (build-cea Convention 2), read by every US model for a 2024-25 year.

rows.label: Value of an hour of volunteer time, United States, 2025 (US$)

source.title: Independent Sector and the Do Good Institute, Value of Volunteer Time
source.quote: the estimate for the value of a volunteer hour was $36.14 in 2025, a 3.9% increase from 2024

rows.explainer: The same for 2025 (preliminary): the US wage plus fringe benefits, for models of a 2025 year.

rows.label: Spending of the second-lowest-income fifth of US households, as a share of the average household's, 2024

source.title: BLS, Consumer Expenditures in 2024 (news release, 19 December 2025), Table C: average annual expenditures by income quintile
source.note: All consumer units $78,535; second quintile $50,054; 50,054 / 78,535 = 0.6374. Per consumer unit; per person the ratio depends on the households' size.

rows.explainer: How much less the second-poorest fifth of US households spend than the average one, per household: the anchor for clients of US services aimed at modest working incomes (about 50% to 80% of the area median), such as affordable homeownership.

rows.label: Household spending per person, United States, 2024 (Consumer Expenditure Survey, US$)

source.title: BLS, Consumer Expenditures in 2024 (news release, 19 December 2025), Table C; people per consumer unit from the same survey (BLS via FRED, CXU980010LB0101M)
source.quote: Average annual expenditures for all consumer units in 2024 were $78,535
source.note: People per consumer unit, all consumer units, 2024: 2.4 (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/data/CXU980010LB0101M). 78,535 / 2.4 = 32,723.

rows.explainer: What an average person in the United States spends in a year by the household survey: below the national accounts' consumption per person (consumption_per_person_2024, the base of the site's rich-country models), which also counts employer- and government-paid health care, owners' imputed rent and non-profits' spending. Read only where a model has to say how that gap is shared between poorer and better-off households.
